problem:
Solstice Bank released a new corporate payment channel that lets customers submit salary and supplier payments through an API. In the first week after release, the operations team notices duplicate debits: several corporate customers have been charged twice for the same instruction, and a few suppliers have been paid twice. The pattern is not random. Duplicates cluster around slow channel responses, where the customer system timed out, retried the submission, and both attempts were processed as separate payments. The release also changed the retry behaviour of an internal event consumer, so some events are now redelivered and processed a second time. Customers are asking for their money back, the finance team wants to know how many duplicates exist, and the release team wants to know whether to roll back.

The learner must investigate as an operations and controls problem, not only as a code defect. The core question is how the platform distinguishes a technical retry from a genuine second payment, and what happens when that distinction fails. The answer involves idempotency keys, payload hashes, duplicate detection rules, durable state and a recovery process that returns money exactly once. The case also tests the discipline of not silently discarding ambiguous payments: an uncertain match must go to review, never to an automatic delete or an automatic re-post.
solution:
Start by containing the failure: confirm whether duplicates are still being created and, if so, stop the affected path or route it through a manual check. Then establish the affected population using stable identifiers rather than guesswork: match on idempotency key, instruction reference, end-to-end identification, debtor, creditor, amount, currency and value date, and separate confirmed duplicates from uncertain matches. For confirmed duplicates, reverse the second financial effect exactly once through the controlled reversal process, with a unique reversal reference linked to the original payment, and confirm the customer account and the supplier position. Uncertain matches go to a review worklist with maker-checker approval; they are never silently discarded or automatically re-posted.

Then fix the cause at each layer. Persist the idempotency key with the payload hash, the original payment reference, timestamps and outcome, so a retry with the same key returns the original reference and creates no second debit. Apply duplicate detection using stable business identifiers, but do not rely on amount and beneficiary alone, because two genuine identical payments are possible. Make event redelivery idempotent so a redelivered event updates state once. Define the retention and replay policy for idempotency records, and add monitoring that alerts on duplicate detection events and on retries after timeouts. Finally, re-run the affected population check after the fix to prove no new duplicates are being created, and report the count, the value and the recovery status to finance and to affected customers.

decision.question: Solstice Bank released a new corporate payment API. In the first week, customers report duplicate debits: slow channel responses led to retries that were processed as separate payments, and an event consumer redelivers some events. You are the business analyst leading the investigation and the recovery.

options.label: A
options.detail: Block all retries in the channel, since retries are the cause of the problem.

options.label: B
options.detail: Tell customers to submit a new payment to replace the duplicate, since the money will sort itself out in reconciliation.

options.label: C
options.detail: Stop the duplicate path, identify every affected payment with idempotency and reference data, reverse duplicates exactly once through a controlled process, and fix idempotency, deduplication and redelivery handling.

options.label: D
options.detail: Delete the second debit from the ledger directly, since it is obviously a duplicate.

decisionRationale: Option C is correct because it contains the failure, identifies the full affected population, corrects each duplicate exactly once, and fixes the control that failed. Option B creates a third payment. Option D deletes a financial record without an audited reversal. Option A removes a legitimate recovery mechanism and leaves genuine timeouts with no safe path.

steps.title: Contain the duplicate path and open the incident record
Define matching rules and identify confirmed duplicates and uncertain matches
Reverse confirmed duplicates exactly once with linked reversal references
Persist idempotency keys with payload hash and original reference
Make event redelivery idempotent and add duplicate alerts
Re-run the population check after the fix and report recovery status
Notify affected customers with the reversal reference and date

happy: Duplicates stop being created, every confirmed duplicate is reversed exactly once with a linked reference, uncertain matches are resolved through review, and the idempotency and redelivery controls are proven by a clean re-run of the population check. Customers receive a clear statement of what was reversed and when.

negative.title: Same key with altered payload
negative.detail: A retry arrives with the same idempotency key but different amount or beneficiary. Reject the request as a key conflict, return an error, and route it for review rather than creating a payment.

negative.title: Retry after timeout
negative.detail: The channel times out, the customer retries, and the first attempt later completes. Return the original reference for the same key so the retry is recognised as the same instruction.

negative.title: Duplicate detected after downstream submission
negative.detail: The duplicate is found only after the second payment has left the bank. Reverse through the controlled process with a linked reversal reference and reconcile the supplier position.

negative.title: Concurrent requests
negative.detail: Two identical requests arrive at the same moment before either is persisted. Use a durable uniqueness constraint on the idempotency key so only one request creates the payment.

technical: Persist the idempotency key scoped to the initiating party and instruction, the payload hash, the original payment ID, the timestamps and the outcome, and keep those records for the agreed retention period. Store the duplicate detection rules with their version and effective date, and log every duplicate detection event, reversal and review decision with operator, timestamp and reason. Keep the original and the reversal linked by reference so the audit trail shows exactly one financial effect per genuine instruction.

accounting: Each duplicate is a second debit to the customer account and a second credit to the supplier, so the reversal must credit the customer and, where the supplier was overpaid, recover or offset the second credit through the agreed process. Reversals go through suspense only where the standard process requires it, and each reversal is reconciled separately from the original payment so finance can prove the customer is whole. Operations need a duplicate worklist with ageing and service levels, a daily count and value of duplicates detected, and a rule that no operator reverses a payment without a linked original reference and a second approval for large values.

scenarios.then: the platform returns the original payment reference and does not create a second debit.

scenarios.given: two payments share amount and beneficiary,
scenarios.when: they carry different idempotency keys and references,
scenarios.then: they are treated as potentially genuine and routed for review rather than automatically discarded.
the customer account is credited exactly once with a reversal reference linked to the original payment.

questions.question: How do you distinguish a technical retry from a genuine second payment?
options: By the idempotency key and stable instruction identifiers
questions.explanation: An idempotency key scoped to the initiating party and instruction, with the payload hash and original reference, identifies a retry; amount and beneficiary alone cannot, because two genuine identical payments are possible.

questions.question: What should happen to an uncertain duplicate match?
options: Route it to a review worklist with maker-checker approval
questions.explanation: An ambiguous payment must never be silently discarded or automatically re-posted; it goes to review with an audited decision.

questions.question: Why is a direct ledger delete the wrong way to fix a duplicate debit?
options: It changes the supplier balance only
It removes the financial record without an audited reversal linked to the original
questions.explanation: A duplicate must be corrected through a controlled reversal with a linked reference, so the audit trail proves exactly one financial effect per genuine instruction.

questions.question: What makes event redelivery safe?
options: Idempotent processing so a redelivered event updates state once
questions.explanation: Idempotent event handling ensures a redelivered event does not create a second payment or a second debit.
